ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin acidusbor. French acidebor. English acid From French acide, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”), from aceō (“to be sour”). Doublet of agita.

senses.d: Sour, sharp, or biting to the taste; tart; having the taste of vinegar.

ex: His response was harsh and acid.
His voice was as stern and his face as acid as ever.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to an acid; acidic.
Denoting a musical genre that is a distortion (as if hallucinogenic) of an existing genre, as in acid house, acid jazz, acid rock.
Any compound which yields H+ ions (protons) when dissolved in water; an Arrhenius acid.
Any compound that easily donates protons to a base; a Brønsted acid.
Any compound that can accept a pair of electrons to form a covalent bond; a Lewis acid.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French aigre, from Vulgar Latin ācrus (possibly via a southern Gallo-Romance dialect), from Latin ācer (with a change in declension), from Proto-Italic *akris, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós (“sharp”). Doublet of âcre, which was borrowed from Latin.
Borrowed from Latin acidus (“acid”), from aceō (“to be sour”).
